utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest last night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to continue? Thank you. Mr. Re, please continue with your direct examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Will do, thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Re: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Alispahic. I want to remind you of where we were up to yesterday before we broke. And you were telling the Trial Chamber about your meeting Mr. Emin Zebic, Jablanica police station, and him telling you about a massacre of civilians committed by members, he had been told, of the Sarajevo units in that area. Yesterday you said it was, you were told, in a village. What was the name of that village?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I didn't say I was told in a village, I was just told it was in some village, and this is what I was told at the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told, do you remember now, the name of the place where the massacre occurred?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the village of Grabovica. That's what the village was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you heard of this village of Grabovica before your conversation that day with Mr. Zebic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first time I was told about that village. I had never been to that village before the incident or crime or after. I located it on a map. It's a village down the river Neretva. That's as much as I know. I know that the population of the village was predominantly Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you locate it on the map? Was it that time or some later point?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got interested in finding out about its location. No common citizen would find the village particularly important, I think. It's just a village down by the side of the road, as simple as that. So I saw it later on a map. The police in their - what should I call it? - work use maps. So you can read the name of this village on a map and find out about its location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Zebic, who else was there when he was speaking to you about the massacre in this village?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any names. I think the commander was there and some of his associates. There were two or three people, perhaps. Emin Zebic and two or three of his associates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Mr. Halilovic when you were speaking to Mr. Zebic that morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I'm not sure if the witness said he was speaking that morning, but I might have missed something last time, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we have the time frame established first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought you said "morning" yesterday, I just can't find it. It was in my mind and I thought I read it there this morning. If there's any doubt about this, when, what time of day did you have this meeting with Mr. Zebic; morning, afternoon, night?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning hours. Not too early, though. In the morning hours when - what should I call them? - work activities are resumed, or perhaps I should call them normal activities. It was in the morning, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Mr. Halilovic when you were having this meeting with Mr. Zebic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was at the police station, that is when we were talking, something happened and I don't know where General Halilovic was. I really didn't know where he was staying at all, or where he was at that moment, for that matter. However, when I asked, Mr. Zebic offered a phone for me to use to try and track down Mr. Halilovic in order to speak to him and in order to arrange for a meeting over that issue. Zebic dialled a number somewhere and found General Halilovic. So it was from the police station that I had this phone conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying there that you asked Mr. Zebic to find Mr. Halilovic for you?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I asked Mr. Zebic, and I think that was only logical because Zebic knew who was where and what was where in Jablanica. It was much easier for him to track people down than for me. He knew where people were staying, and I was just passing through. I didn't have that kind of information. Zebic knew where the command was, where certain phones were that were still operational, who was manning the phones. I didn't have that sort of information myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why did you want to speak to Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to tell him what I had been told by the Jablanica police. I wanted to look at what the options were. I wanted to do something as a police officer. I wanted to say that these things must be dealt with, either by the army or the police. I wanted light shed on the matter and the case explained. That was the main reason why I wanted to see the general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you want to speak to that particular general as opposed to any other senior military officer who may have been in the area?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of his position, General Halilovic was the Chief of Staff, which means the number two man of the entire army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Secondly, I believed or I knew or I understood that General Halilovic was the commander of the operation that was underway and that he was the person who had all the information. In the context of everything that was - how shall I put it? - going on on the ground, including potential incidents and crimes, the logic I used was firstly the hierarchy, the chain of command, and secondly, the fact that - to use plain language - Mr. Halilovic was the boss of the operation. Ultimately, I think in the brief communication that I had I realised that all the other commanders who were with General Halilovic displayed the same sort of attitude towards him; they accepted him as the person in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which brief communication are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brief conversation during my stay. That means later when I had left the police station and arrived in the area of the forward command post. We had a talk, and there were other officers there, and I realised that that group of people had business of their own with General Halilovic. The result was that my stay there was rather short, so this is the time frame I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll move to that in a moment. If I could just take you back now. You said you believed or understood that General Halilovic was the commander of the operation that was underway and that he had -- he was the person who had all the information. What was it that led you to understand on that particular day that Mr. Halilovic was the commander of that operation that was underway?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that was going on after the meeting in Zenica and the talks that were held in Zenica, the resubordination of the special unit to the BH army, and for the most part General Halilovic's statement or speech about the needs of the military, and those needs truly were justified. Also, the conversations I had with a number of different commanders, such as General Delic and other commanders. It was based on these that I realised - and this is only logical if you look at the way my mind works - that General Halilovic was in charge as far as that area and that particular activity was concerned. And when I say "activity" I mean two concepts. I mean that he as the number one man of this operation should have been familiar with what was going on; and secondly, he was the number two man in the army and in the area he was the most senior officer in terms of position and thus be the one who would have been expected to solve any problems. And this is to explain why I spoke to the general directly and why we had this communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to a statement or speech General Halilovic had given about the needs of the military. Which speech are you referring to? Was that at Zenica or some other town?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zenica, yes. The consideration, the definition of activity. In relation to the Neretva action, I think we can now address it like that because the action was called Neretva 93. It was in Zenica that the reasons and needs were defined. Quite simply, all the elements to do with the start of the action were defined there, at that meeting, I believe. While I was there, the first day of the meeting, and I think later, since the meeting lasted some time, in a purely operative sense these things were defined with a greater degree of precision and probably prepared in terms of documents being drafted, units being assigned; everything that an army normally does in its work, in its work technology, if you like. There was a great amount of activity to be done. It wasn't easy to move those units about or bring them to the area. It wasn't easy to ensure they had sufficient supplies. Even if this was -- even if this had been, for example, a peacetime activity, it would have been complicated enough. In this sort of situation, it was yet more complex and more difficult, and it required a lot of activity and a lot of obligations. So from that very meeting, I'm trying to, as they say, get things in some sort of order, I realised that General Halilovic was the commander of the operation that was about to begin, and that was the reason I addressed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said a few moments ago that your understanding that he was in charge of -- the commander of that operation was also based upon conversations you had with a number of different commanders, such as General Delic and other commanders. I want you to tell the Trial Chamber about your conversations with General Delic and other commanders which led you to believe that General Halilovic was in charge of that operation.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I've given you the first and principal reasons: The presentation and the defining of the need for the operation to take place, which was at the meeting. After this meeting, when I spoke to specifically General Delic, he said that General Halilovic personally would be in charge of the operation, that he had every authorisation to mobilise all the supplies and equipment as well as units needed and that he -- it would be made possible for him to successfully run these combat activities. So that's as far as I remember. That's what I spoke to Delic about. In this environment where the military structure was, the command structure, for example, Vehbija Karic, I'm not sure about his rank and position at the time, but he was a high-ranking officer; for example, Zicro Suljevic, Bilajac, they were generals, I assume, but they would be addressed as "boss" or "commander" in that context because this was a situation where there was a quick succession of changes in the army. General Halilovic was first commander and suddenly became chief. It was a sort of inertia that was involved in these changes. So people would address him as "boss" or "commander," and everything they wanted to make sure about, they would go to General Halilovic. As to what people wanted to make sure about, this is not something that I went into. I didn't think it was fair to go into that sort of thing, so I didn't. I'm just trying to explain to you what the environment was and what the relations were, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going back to your conversation with General Rasim Delic, do you remember how long after the Zenica meeting and before your units went to Herzegovina you had this conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had frequent conversations in Sarajevo. It was very often necessary to get in touch with General Delic. There were many reasons, there were many problems, and these problems had to be tackled. So we were in a situation where we had all the problems that I testified about yesterday, a situation that I described, and now there was this task that we had to deal with in some way. So I would meet General Delic nearly several times a week. We would have a conversation. We would meet in the overall context of tackling these problems and especially the relationship between the army and the police. And everything that I -- official positions implied in terms of solving problems, Delic told me that this was underway, that some of the units had been transferred and some hadn't. He was asking me whether I had prepared units for dispatch and whether I had received an information on these current problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "problems," are you referring to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your last answer you referred to meeting General Delic several times a week. "We would meet in the overall context of tackling these problems..." the relationship between the army and the police. And he asked you whether you had prepared units for dispatch "and whether I had received any information -- an information on these current problems." What I want to know is: What are you referring to when you say "problems"?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood. It was not in the context of the problems that Delic asked about the unit. When we asked about those matters, he wanted to know whether I had prepared what I took upon myself as the duty to allocate a special unit for that operation. This is what I was referring to. And as for the problems, we discussed them in general terms, the problems that existed in Sarajevo and how to solve them. So let us not link up these two matters. He wanted to know whether I indeed carried out everything that I had taken upon myself in the context of this operation. Quite another matter are the activities that were conducted in Sarajevo regarding the problems in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "operation," are you still referring to the operation in Herzegovina which you came to know as Operation Neretva?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just move back to the telephone call that Mr. Zebic made to General Halilovic on the morning from Jablanica police station. You said you spoke to Mr. Halilovic. What did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a very brief conversation, just long enough in order to identify who was there in order to discuss what I wanted to discuss. So basically, this was not a proper conversation; we simply spoke about where and when we could meet. And the general said that it would be best if I came to the hydroelectric plant in Jablanica, where the forward command post was located. I think that "the forward command post" is a military term which denotes a type of a command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell him why you wanted to meet him?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I said anything on the phone about the reasons for meeting him. I think that I simply said, "I wish to meet you. There are certain problems or reasons for the meeting." I might have given him some more detailed explanation, but I simply cannot recall that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after the telephone call to Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately following the conversation, I went to the premises which are located nearby. I arrived in those premises. Right at the entrance, at the gate, I think, there was a soldier who was there to secure the area. Then I came into a room where there were officers, including General Halilovic. I think that Zicro Suljevic, Vehbija Karic were there as well, as was possibly Officer Bilajac and perhaps several more senior officers, not too many of them. This was the room which was used as the room for the forward command post, and this was within the hydroelectric power plant Jablanica. This room formerly used to be a conference room and at that time was used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of things were in this room?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a long table with chairs around it, and then on one wall there was a board or something like that. I'm not sure what was underneath, but there were maps covering it with military markings. I assume that they depicted the deployment or positions of forces in that area of Herzegovina. I did not read those maps, as they say in the military, so I couldn't really tell you what they depicted, what they showed. I simply was close enough to realise that these were military maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness just be shown for a moment Exhibit D134, which is the large map which is behind me there. I actually said D134; I meant D131.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, I just want you to have a look at that map. You said you saw some maps on the wall, military-type maps. All I want you to do, when this map is pinned up, is just tell the Trial Chamber whether --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will -- whether you recognise this particular map, this one here, as the one that was on the wall - that's the first part - and secondly, whether -- what you can say about this map in relation to the types of maps you saw on the wall in the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't claim with certainty that this was precisely this map that I saw on the wall, this map that is in front of me now. Based on what I saw in view of the situation that I was in, in view of the distance between me and the maps, I couldn't claim with full certainty that this was precisely this map. As for the nature and type of map, in view of my experience during the war with the military and with the police, and in view of my experience with working with the maps and so on, I can tell you that this is a typical military map showing the position of the forces of the HV, HVO, and the BH army. I think that other important things are marked on the map as well, such as combat disposition, disposition of the weaponry, equipment, the direction of activities. I think that military commands typically have these sorts of maps, and I think that they're changed, sometimes on a daily basis, and that any changes are entered into the map. Whenever there are changes on the ground, changes are entered into maps as well. If we look at the name of the operation, which is normally placed in the heading of the map --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not actually after an opinion as to this particular map. All I want to know is whether maps of a similar type to this one were on the wall in the IKM when you were there.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were military maps with certain information that I just described to you, information that every military map should have. Such type of military maps must be present in all environments where combat operations are conducted, even in lower-ranking command posts, let alone high command posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier when you were telling the Trial Chamber about why you understood Mr. Halilovic was in charge of the operation was that when you were at the meeting at the IKM there was something about the attitude the other commanders who were with General Halilovic displayed towards him when you were there, that also led you to believe that he was in charge. And I want you to tell the Trial Chamber what you observed about the behaviour of the other people in the IKM that day towards General Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this will be a sufficient explanation, but in institutions such as the army or the police one can see clearly who is the boss and who isn't because of the type of communication that exists between people. In the army, the command system is of major importance because it reflects the position of the superior. The general was the Chief of Staff, therefore I had no doubt about the fact that he was the number one man in that environment, in that structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the others there behaving towards him? What they -- how were they addressing him? How was he addressing them?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I didn't spend -- I didn't stay long enough there to have a full picture, what I could tell you was that the officers who were there - and I don't know anything about their ranks - they reported to the general, they briefed him on what was going on, and they listened to what he was saying and ordering. If I addressed the general as the number one man, then I did that because I wanted to speak with the right person about whatever problem I had. I did not think that I should talk to Vehbija Karic. I think that from my point of view that would have been irrelevant. My reading was that General Halilovic was the head of that operation, both in terms of the essence and the form. And I've already explained to you what I am referring to when I say "the essence and the form."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you and Mr. Halilovic address each other? You were the minister of the interior and he was the Chief of Staff -- chief of the Main Staff of the army.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that their relations were proper, decent human relations. I thought that I was in the position to tell everything to the general, and vice versa, that he could also say everything to me. We were not on too formal terms. I myself was not a member of the military, therefore the military subordination did not apply to me. Moreover, the -- my relationship with the general was such that it was not too formal. We believed that in direct communication we would be able to solve the problems quicker and that the more efficient communication would be in favour of that, therefore our communication was a proper one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say to him in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived there, there were several senior officers and the general present. I think they were discussing some military matters and issues. I don't know what it was about. I arrived there and I started by saying, General, such-and-such problem has occurred, I have been informed by the police station about that, the problem could be a major one, we don't know of its extent right now. I believe that this should not have happened and I propose that we establish the facts and take appropriate measures in order to take disciplinary action. I think that the general was already partially or perhaps even fully informed about what had happened. I realised that he saw this as a major problem, that he was not indifferent to it. After this conversation, if I can call it that, I wanted, in my capacity as minister of police, to inform him about what had happened and to hold the perpetrators accountable, perpetrators of that incident or crime. I wanted to inform General Halilovic of this. The general most likely considered this, and I think that on that occasion he told me that the military would resolve it with its own resources, that there was no need for police to interfere, and that it was possible for the perpetrators of the crime to also create an incident with the policemen. I understood that and I believed it to be a reasonable solution and I offered any kind of assistance. By that, I mean professional assistance within the means available to the police. I said that if anything was needed, the police would provide it. I think that then another officer intervened; it might have been Vehbija Karic. My reaction was that these people ought to be sent back to Sarajevo and disciplined, that they ought to be removed from the area in order to avoid any further incidents or similar situations. That was the gist, the summary, of my visit to the area, meeting with the general and the others. We did not discuss the event itself any further. We did not discuss any of these matters. And after staying there briefly, I left the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you arrived there and started by saying, "General, such-and-such a problem has occurred. I have been informed by the police station about the problem; it could be a major one." Then you said that you think -- you thought that the general was already partially or perhaps fully informed about what had happened. I just want to clarify that a little bit. Did you tell General Halilovic what Mr. Zebic had told you about what had happened in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conveyed to the general what I knew, what I had learned from Emin Zebic. I think that when we talked about that, about that problem, the crime in Grabovica, neither I nor General Delic or Zebic had full information, full insight into what had happened in Grabovica. We simply heard about the crime, about the incident. We heard about that, were informed of that, received information that it was impossible to access the area. The operative information indicated that a large number of people were killed; 20, 30 were the numbers mentioned, that the victims included civilians, the elderly, women, and so on. However, the entire information, all of the details, were not known at the time. That was what the situation was like when we talked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much information did it appear to you that General Halilovic had about what had happened in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not establish that. I think I've just told you that I think that even he did not know the proportion of the crime at the time when we talked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your attitude then towards the continued participation of your Laste Unit in that particular operation?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident which took place there was the straw that broke the camel's back in terms of the incident caused by the army members, by certain individuals. This was really the last drop, and I was revolted. I was appalled. Therefore, I said that when it comes to that operation, the Neretva operation, which was to liberate that entire territory all the way up to Mostar, I said that I would not allow the Laste Unit to continue its participation in the operation. That unit could participate in military combat and so on. It was deployed in Mostar, but after the incident took place, I told the general and his associates - and I repeated that later on to Delic - that I was against it and that I would not permit the special unit to participate in the operation any further. I think that I was still under the heavy impression, I was still quite emotional because of this incident and what had happened. I even proposed that the operation be suspended until the facts were established. I was concerned that these people could continue with this type of behaviour and that they could continue with similar "military operations." This was the reason for my reaction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Halilovic's reaction, response, to your saying you wanted to withdraw your units from the operation?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say I assume it was not relevant to him at the time because not a lot of members of the special unit were involved. 50 men is not a lot. It is quite a number of men but it's not crucial and it wouldn't bring any commander to change his decision. I think the general decided to go on with the military operation and that he would discipline the people, the members of the army. I don't think he thought it was a good idea just to halt the operation, and again I must say this was something that was a matter of military assessment and there was a decision to continue these operations in order to liberate the areas under consideration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Halilovic respond when you said you wanted to withdraw your units from the operation? You just said a moment ago you could assume it wasn't relevant to him. What I'm after is: Do you remember whether he responded to you?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember whether he provided a specific answer to what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown photograph 0299-2334, which is Exhibit Number 147 on our 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 432.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume this is an aerial photograph, which means that it was taken from a plane. The photograph of Jablanica, the -- a general view of the urban structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see the building where the forward command post was located in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you follow the road into the town of Jablanica itself, it's on the left-hand side --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll get you to mark it on the map. My question is: Can you see it there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you just --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The water plant of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to put a circle around that building.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just underneath it can you please write "IKM" on the screen.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be received into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There's no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The original photograph will be Prosecution Exhibit P432, and the one that's marked now will be Prosecution Exhibit P433.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you attend that meeting with?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think General Halilovic was there, Vehbija Karic, Zicro Suljevic, Bilajac, and some other officers whose names I can't remember now. But there weren't too many officers there because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, what I actually mean -- because? I'm sorry. I cut you off mid-sentence.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were many officers at the forward command post at the time, and that is the reason I can't remember too many names. I have now told you about the people I'm sure were there, people I saw. I think throughout the operation they were there, for the operation itself and in order to deal with other military matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I was actually asking you -- what I meant was: Did you attend the meeting by yourself or did you go with someone? Did someone accompany you there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I arrived on my own with my driver and my vehicle. I knew where the forward command post was, or rather I was told to go there because that was the place. I had never been to the area before. I didn't even know it was there; I only knew where the police station was in Jablanica. I came. I was there on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go after that meeting with Mr. Halilovic at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some other minor duties to see to in Jablanica and later in Konjic. I was meeting the former BH government minister, Rusmir Mahmutcehajic [Realtime transcript read in error "Ahmutcehajic"], later on in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P118.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think this was written properly, Rusmir Ahmutcehajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will correct that in the transcript later, Mr. Alispahic. Thank you for pointing it out. Do you have the document on the screen there in front of you? It's a document dated the 9th of September, 1993, headed "Order," directed to the 4th Corps Commander Mostar, saying: "Please inform the minister of internal affairs, Bakir Alispahic, to head to Jablanica tonight because he has a meeting tomorrow, 10th of September, 1993, at 1900 hours in Konjic with Mr. Rusmir Mahmutcehajic," and the name Sefer Halilovic, chief of the Supreme Command staff. A moment ago you said you were due to have a meeting with Mr. Mahmutcehajic. Does that document refer to the meeting you were to have with him?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document informing me about the precise time. Before I left Sarajevo for Herzegovina, I had had an appointment with Minister Mahmutcehajic that we would meet in that area, without defining the exact time, that he would resolve matters that were in his remit. And then the 4th Corps informed me about the exact place and time of our meeting. Nothing had been agreed ahead of time and it was in that day, in the afternoon, and here it says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the time that the witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that we were supposed to meet. I have never seen this document before because at the time I was informed orally that I was to meet at such-and-such a time. It was an oral report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interpreters missed the time which you specified. Did you say 1900 hours, as it says in that document?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just read it from here, from the document. It says, "1930."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does -- or do the dates on that document accord with your memory of when it was that you met Mr. Mahmutcehajic and Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date simply must be right. This is a document, after all. It's a generally known fact that Minister Mahmutcehajic was a very accurate person and I am sure that was when the meeting took place; there's no doubt about that. I mean, Mahmutcehajic never postponed or delayed any of his meetings. I think the date and time must be right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you meet Mr. Mahmutcehajic on that day after meeting Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had this working meeting. We had an appointment. Mr. Mahmutcehajic was dealing with important things at the time. He was the minister for energy resources. He was in charge of supplying the army with sources of energy, and the police, too, in a way. And he wanted to help to the extent that he could. Further, the minister also dealt with special-purpose industry. In Konjic we had a production line for infantry ammunition, so I visited the factory with Mahmutcehajic. He spoke to engineers, he spoke to the manager and people at the factory about the problems that he was dealing with. Mahmutcehajic was billeted in a military installation near Konjic, and that's where we had the meeting, that's where we dealt with the matters that he had delegated to us, in a manner of speaking, that we were supposed to come to grips with. All these matters were related to a variety of military activities; that's what it was about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there -- are you referring to one or two meetings with him on that day?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure there was only one meeting on that day. There can't have been two meetings. All of us who were involved in defence had many meetings with Mahmutcehajic. There were always problems to be solved. We were always short of ammunition, of petrol, and he was the person who could help obtain those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, are you saying that you visited the munition factory with him and then had a meeting later with him at the accommodation facility for the military?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that it was the next day that I was with him at the factory, or rather I think it was on the same day and it was later in the afternoon that we had this - what should I call it? - official meeting. When I returned from Jablanica, I came to the Konjic police station. I learned that there were things going on in Konjic, that Mahmutcehajic had already arrived. And I think it was later on in the day, before the meeting, that we went to this special-purpose factory. I can't be positive about this, the timing, but what I'm positive about is that the meetings took place in the setting that I've described; that much is certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The meeting you're referring to, who was at the meeting? Was Mr. Halilovic there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he had a lot of his own business to see to, but he came to the meeting. And the focus of the meeting was on issues of relevance to Minister Mahmutcehajic, what he was dealing with. I think a number of Mahmutcehajic's associates were there, I was there, General Halilovic was there, possibly also Vehbija Karic or some other generals and associates, someone from the military logistics department. There was discussion, and issues were being tackled related to the supply of logistics for continuing combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the events in Grabovica discussed?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events were discussed, but one thing I wish to point out is that they were not discussed in relation to other issues discussed at that meeting. It was an informal discussion because one did not know exactly what had happened. Information was incomplete. I think both General Halilovic and I talked to Mahmutcehajic about what had happened. At least I can speak for myself. I was surprised by the crime. I couldn't bring myself to accept it. I talked to General Halilovic about this. I gave the police station certain tasks related to this, and believed that any steps should be taken to overcome this situation and tackle the problem. I believed this was something that should never have happened to the BH army. Mahmutcehajic was also surprised. He was also surprised and reacted in a way to show his disapproval. He wanted to establish what exactly had happened and for the perpetrators to be punished. Normally he was not a man who interfered much or understood much about combat operations, but his reaction was purely human. And once the conversation was over and I was leaving for Sarajevo, he said that I should inform the president and General Delic about this because this was not a matter that should be passed over lightly, this was not a matter that should go unsolved, and this was a matter that should be looked into. That's what Rusmir said and that's what Rusmir felt about this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your intention to see President Izetbegovic and General Delic about this matter?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no doubt then, and I still have no doubt now, that I should do it. I believe that I, as someone who had been to the area, should go to these people to inform them, to the extent that I could, to share whatever information I could with them, and to insist that the matter be explained and resolved. That was my intention. That's what I had in mind at the time. And I still believe this was the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you communicate your intention to see President Izetbegovic and General Delic to Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I don't remember ever telling him that I would go and see these people about what had happened. I believed that General Halilovic would use his own contacts within the army to pass the information on. I did what I believed I was supposed to do in my capacity at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be a little bit more clear about this: Where was this meeting held, the second meeting you had with Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Rusmir Mahmutcehajic and Halilovic and the logistics people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that one.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a military facility called Arka. This is near Konjic. It's a rather large military installation, built to the best military standards in terms of security and in terms of how it met its purpose. There are certain outbuildings there with meeting rooms, conference rooms, and the meeting took place in one of those buildings next to the river Neretvica. It was a working meeting and that was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you return to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably returned that night. Why am I saying probably that night? Because you could only go into Sarajevo by night. During the day it would have been impossible on account of the ongoing combat operations that made it impossible to enter or leave Sarajevo. So you couldn't negotiate the road into Sarajevo over Mount Igman because it would have been a life-threatening journey. Many people lost their lives along that route. So it was at night that I entered Sarajevo, and the next day I was back at work and went to see the people that I've told you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I neglected to ask you something a moment ago, and that was: Do you remember seeing Sefko Hodzic when you were in Jablanica or Konjic on the day you met both Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Rusmir Mahmutcehajic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere or other, in Konjic I think, I met the journalist Hodzic in passing. I think we had an informal chat. He asked me where I was headed to and what I was doing, and I think I told him I was going to a meeting organised by Rusmir Mahmutcehajic; that was that. Sefko Hodzic, during the military operations in the area, dispatched reports to the media in Sarajevo, and these media then announced which positions the BH army had taken and reported any military successes. So Sefko Hodzic was the person behind this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's almost 10.30, Your Honours. Is that an appropriate time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's take a break and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We are now at the position, Mr. Alispahic, when you went to speak to Mr. Delic. I'm going to ask you about your meeting with Mr. Delic and your meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic. Firstly, you said you returned to Sarajevo, and the next day, after your meeting with Mr. Halilovic, you went and saw Mr. Delic. Why did you go and see Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason for me to go in the morning hours - I'm not sure what time exactly it was but it was in the morning hours - to go to the command where General Delic was, was to inform him about the information that I had learned during my stay in Herzegovina and in Jablanica. I told him that I had received the basic information from the chief of the police station. Then I told him what I had heard while at the police station, told him that I had informed General Halilovic about it, and that I had talked to Rusmir about it in Konjic. And that, finally, I told him that I had come to inform him about that as well because we had such a good relationship that I thought that I could tell him about what I knew and also warn him that that problem needed to be resolved. For my own peace of mind, I wanted to inform the general personally about this; that was my position. I stayed briefly with the general, perhaps half an hour, and during that time we did not discuss this problem alone. There were some other issues as well. General Delic made it known to me that he knew some of that information; however, it was not my impression that he knew a lot, and it seemed as though he was not aware of the full scope of the problem, just as I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his response to your visit and your telling him about the information you'd received about what happened in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that he was upset - I don't know whether that was the right term - that he regretted this. His reaction was such that I realised that his position was that this should not have happened, that this was a disgrace, and that this was something impermissible. This was the impression that I received. He said that he would personally ask that this be inquired into and that he would personally see to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever communicate to you that he had in fact ordered that it be inquired into?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After our meeting, in the following days we would see each other occasionally for various reasons, in order to solve various issues, issues that fell under our jurisdiction. Therefore, I can't claim this with certainty, however, the general did say that he had issued an order that this be looked into. He wanted to receive more information -- or rather, I asked him whether he received more information, more reliable information about it, and he said, "I took certain steps in that direction. I sent a dispatch." That's what he told me. I didn't know what the dispatch was about, but I understood that this was to do with the incident and that this was most likely an order that he issued in order to have this case investigated and the facts established.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit D157.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that's coming, was there anyone else present at that meeting you had with Mr. Delic or was it just the two of you?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you turn to the document to the left, on your screen, it's an order dated the 12th of September, 1993, with Rasim Delic's name on the bottom of it. Now, you said a moment ago that you understood that he had issued an order. Have you seen this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's not accurately putting what was put. Your Honours, he said that he was told that a dispatch was -- well, Your Honours know what was said. He said: "I asked him whether he received more information, more reliable information about it, and he said, 'I took certain steps in that direction. I sent a dispatch.' That's what he told me. I didn't know what the dispatch was about, but I understood that this was to do with the incident and that this was most likely an order that he issued in order to have this case investigated and the facts established." That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's how I paraphrased it, I said he understood that an order was issued, which is a paraphrase of that line, "I understood this was to do with the incident and most likely an order that he issued..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Hopefully your paraphrase is in line of whatever the witness said. Hopefully you could do it again, taking into consideration the objections put by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will re-quote back exactly, rather than paraphrase. It will take longer, but I'll certainly do it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alispahic, a moment ago you said: "He told me --" "... he said, 'I took certain steps in that direction. I sent a dispatch.' That's what he told me. I don't know what the dispatch was about but I understood that this was to do with the incident and this was most likely an order he issued in order to have the case investigated and the facts established." Now, moving from what you said a few moments ago back to the document --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to explain this in a simple way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can in a moment. I just want to ask you whether you had in fact seen this document before coming to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the information contained in that document accord with your understanding of what Rasim Delic said that he had done?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that question is not permissible, in my submission. The witness has given evidence about what Mr. Delic said. The Tribunal has the order. If the witness has got some knowledge about this, he may have -- he may have something else to say about this document that's relevant, but to ask him whether what he thinks about it is consistent -- or perhaps to use my friend's terms: "Is the information" -- "Does the information accord with your understanding of what Rasim Delic said that he'd done?" Well, that's no more than to say, "Does that document accord with the words of Rasim Delic?" That's not a matter for this witness to answer; it's a matter for the Court to assess in light of all the other matters that you know about. So, in my submission, it's not a permissible question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, and also taking into consideration that the witness testified that he never saw this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I press the question on this basis -- or I press questioning as to whether that is consistent with what Mr. Delic told him on this basis: There has been a Defence attack on this particular document, many unkind things have been said about its provenance along the way, and I must be entitled, in the Prosecution's submission, to ask the witness, given that he's given evidence that Mr. Delic told him that he had issued an order in similar terms to this - I'm paraphrasing - to this document, whether the document -- the terms of the document accord with what Mr. Delic said to him. That's a step the Prosecution must be entitled to make, in our submission, towards establishing the legitimacy of this document without the author of it there. It's another piece of evidence which goes towards establishing the reliability -- or establishing the fact that this is a legitimate document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could go step by step. First establish whether that dispatch includes any orders; secondly, the witness -- you could ask this witness what exactly Mr. Delic said at that moment; thirdly, you show him this document to see whether that is responded to, whatever Mr. Delic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, firstly, when you said "dispatches" earlier, did you mean that to include orders?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my terminology, the terminology that I understand and the one that is applied in the Ministry of the Interior and in the communication means, "dispatch" is a means of communication. One can send different types of document, from orders, instructions, any kind of document can be sent via a dispatch. In this particular case, it was via a dispatch that the general issued an order concerning certain things, and I ask that this be understood properly, the way I said it. I don't know how you interpret this, but I can repeat: A dispatch is just a mechanism for transmitting certain documents, for sending them to somebody. It can be information, it can be an order, it can be an instruction. In this particular case, an order was sent by way of a dispatch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, secondly, try to remember what Mr. Delic told you was in that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honours. This is completely -- it's leading, it misstates what the witness has previously said, and this whole procedure is unfair for -- as a third basis, because the witness is being asked these questions with an order sitting in front of him on the screen, when he gave quite plain evidence before about what he said about it and what he knew about it. He'd said -- he'd given the words -- now, Your Honour gave leave to my friend to ask three questions in a row, and the second one was: What were the exact words he used? And that really -- my friend is, in my submission, seeking to jump over that. That should be the next question, "What were the exact words used by Mr. Delic?"

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that the first part of the question will stand. That is: Try to remember what Mr. Delic told you, first of all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, please try and remember what Mr. Delic told you that he had done, in whatever way he'd done it.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he had sent an order aimed at investigating what had happened in Grabovica and establishing the facts. He sent an order about Grabovica. I can comment on the document, however General Delic said that he had sent an order to investigate the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the third thing His Honour Judge Liu asked me to do is show you the document and ask you whether what is in the document corresponds to what Mr. Delic said.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that what Delic said is consistent with the contents of this order or a dispatch because it contains all the elements pertaining to the investigation. It even gives certain instructions on what to do. I don't know if we need to go into these details right now, but this document contains certain demands sent to the command as to what needs to be done. I think that all of the elements are contained in the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A while back I interrupted you when you said you wanted to explain something. Is there something you still wish to explain about something earlier?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps at the end, once we finish with everything, I would perhaps like to state certain things which are not related to this specific issue. So perhaps we should leave them for the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could perhaps -- what do those issues relate to? Just the subject matter, not the details.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that now. I have these things written down, I have certain things written down related to the activities which took place in accordance with the plans, especially the Trebevic plan. I wanted to point out, I wanted to emphasise, that the plan was verified or approved by the BH Presidency with all of the members present. The operative plan was approved there as well. And General Delic and I simply implemented the Presidency's order concerning the Trebevic plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. We'll -- I will come to that a little later. Now, did -- let's just go back to the meeting with Delic. Yesterday you told the Tribunal that you -- or the Trial Chamber that you and Mr. Delic discussed on a regular basis the problems of the units in Sarajevo. Did you discuss at that particular meeting, when you informed him about Grabovica, the problems of those units in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time because there was not much time. There was no need for that and I was on my way to see the president, so the meeting was very brief and we discussed what I've just described to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your view at the time when you were talking to Mr. Delic on that day, based upon your experience as the police chief in Sarajevo and as the minister of the interior, of the difficulty or otherwise that may be encountered in investigating or attempting to arrest people who were from those units in Sarajevo in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I object to that question. First of all, it's got two questions in it; and secondly, it's got a presumption in it which is not in evidence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry, I withdraw it. It's gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that meeting, you -- did you discuss with Mr. Delic the possibility of arresting -- of having arrested members of the brigades who allegedly committed the massacre in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just again, this has got a presumption in it as well, and the presumption is that there were members of the brigades who allegedly committed the massacre in Grabovica, and in fact the evidence is that there were no identified perpetrators at all at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I regard it also as a compound question. Maybe you could go step by step. I mean, the first part of the question will stand. First you have to establish whether there's any discussions between them. And later on, what's the contents of that discussion?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss with Mr. Delic the identity of those who allegedly committed the crimes in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was clear that the perpetrators of the crime were the members of the army. It was clear to all of us. Initially, we, at least the police, had bare assumptions as to who could have perpetrated that, and it was logical to assume that it could have been done only by the soldiers who were deployed there, who were there to conduct combat operations. So using that logic, we deduced who the perpetrators could have been, or rather members of which units. Our basic aim was to establish the actual perpetrators. We wanted a thorough investigation to be carried out to establish the perpetrators in order to make the job of the military police and other judicial system organs easier. However, there was also a concern that if the perpetrators were not established and not isolated, that the same people could cause another incident, do something similar. In view of the situation and in view of who these people were, they represented a risk for the army and for other army members. This is why I insisted that the problem be taken seriously. This is why I reacted the way I did. From my point of view, the problem had to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm getting at is the identity of the people who committed the massacre, and my learned friend's objection was clearly incorrect a moment ago because the evidence -- this is where I was getting to yesterday at page 72, was that Mr. Zebic told him "there had been operative information to the effect that the army members from Sarajevo - that's what he said - or perhaps members from Celo's and Caco's unit, had ... committed a massacre in a village, and this was the information I received initially." The witness then said that he had conveyed this information to Mr. Halilovic and he had conveyed the information he had received from Mr. Zebic to Mr. Delic, and I was acting on the assumption that he had given that same information, that is, it was Caco and Celo's unit, because that was the evidence here. That was the basis for my putting the questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm getting at, Mr. Alispahic. Did you discuss the fact that -- you said earlier that you gave the information to Mr. Delic that Mr. Zebic had given you. Yesterday you said that Mr. Zebic and you had discussed if it was units or members of Celo and Caco's unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. This has now become a ten-line question. I have done that myself, I have to concede, however, the best thing to do is simply to ask a question, especially when evidence in-chief is being led. A simple question can do. I wouldn't object to asking this, just so that the matter can move on: Was Celo or Caco mentioned in this discussion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, but here this issue has been discussed for several times and it doesn't matter if the Prosecution want to make sure of that. There's no problem on that, because we all know the background for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours are right. But just so that it's clear and so that I'm not seeming to pick a fight, and just so the witness understands, too, what the situation is, when I refer to "perpetrators," I mean killers, I don't mean units from which killers might come. And "perpetrator" means the actual murderer. Now, let it be clear, there has never been any suggestion from Zebic or anyone else that at this stage there were individual perpetrators identified. That was the objection before, and my friend says that's incorrect, well, it's correct. Of course it's right to say that those units had been mentioned. The witness gave that evidence yesterday and that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let us hear the answer from this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the identity of the perpetrators is concerned, I said today in no uncertain terms that we did not have their names at first. This was only logical for the reasons what I've mentioned. The truth is Emin Zebic told me that members of Celo's unit - I think he also said Caco's unit but I'm sure about Celo's unit - were the ones who committed the crime, members of that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you discuss that with Mr. Delic, the fact that you had been told that it was Celo's unit and possibly Caco's unit -- or members of those units who had committed the crimes?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was precisely what I told him, that I'd been there, that I'd heard this, and that people were saying that it was precisely the members of those units that had committed the crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, after seeing Mr. Delic, did you go and see Mr. Izetbegovic, the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After seeing Mr. Delic, and that was a brief meeting, as I've explained, I went straight to the Presidency to see President Izetbegovic, as I had planned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go alone?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it just the two of you there, you and Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you tell Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found Mr. Izetbegovic in his office. I said I was there to inform him about some things that had happened in the field, given the fact that I had arrived from -- back from Herzegovina the night before. In the briefest possible terms, I informed him of what I had learned about and what the chief of the police station had told me. I informed him about that. I told him that I'd spoken to people from the army, General Delic and General Halilovic, and that I was finally now there to inform him, the president. He wanted to know about what had happened. And to the extent that I could, I told him what I'd heard, as I have told you now. He was visibly unsettled. He was visibly upset about this news. And I believe I was the first who broke the news to him. At least, I believed so based on his reaction. The president condemned this in my presence. He was antagonised [as interpreted] by this upon hearing the news, which, by the way, was unverified still but it seemed likely. So he asked his secretary to arrange for a meeting with General Delic. First they spoke on the phone and he told the general that I was there to see him and that he had been informed in very rough terms about the problem. He demanded that the general take a serious approach to resolving this problem. I'm not sure why this was his reaction, but I think he wanted to give an additional warning to the general about the need to shed light on this matter. Roughly speaking, that was the substance of my conversation with the president on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I could just take you back for one moment to the meeting with Rasim Delic, and I'm not sure whether you answered this in passing at some other point. You said that you told Mr. Halilovic the day before that you did not want your units to participate any further in the operation because of what had happened. Did you say something similar to Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told Delic as well that I believed it to be impermissible from my perspective, as well as unnecessary, for special units to be involved in the operation any longer, that I said that they could stay in Mostar for a while, holding the same positions that they were holding at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Delic's response to your saying that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he accepted that. He didn't make any comments, he just said, "Fine."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've -- you've told us about speaking to Mr. Delic, General Delic, the commander-in-chief of the army -- sorry, the commander of the army, and President Izetbegovic. Now, what about the chief of the military security service, Mr. Jasarevic? Did you communicate with him in relation to the events in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the military security -- I wouldn't say that I talked to him. It was more that I asked to inform him about certain matters, to tell him that I'd been to see General Delic and President Izetbegovic. It was a matter of professional courtesy and good relations. That was why I wanted the chief of the military security service, Jasarevic, to know about what I'd done, in order to avoid this move on my part being misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just clarify --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to make sure that he didn't misunderstood what I had done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to clarify what you meant by: "I wouldn't say that I talked to him." Did you actually speak to him, as in a telephone call or a meeting or a letter, in relation to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Jasarevic over the phone at the time, but I didn't speak to him very often. He had an ongoing cooperation with the chief of the state security service, Nedzad Ugljen. They had a professional relationship which entailed a great deal of communication. What I did was merely as an act of courtesy between our two institutions, but we didn't speak about anything specific, really. I believed he would just keep on doing his job. His superiors had been informed, all the relevant people had been informed, therefore, I did not find it necessary to go to the chief of the military security service and explain anything. Information had been exchanged between the state security service and the military security service in relation to what had happened, but in the context of exchanging intelligence and operative information; it was more like that. Later on, I hardly had any communication with Jasarevic, but I did have communication with my own chief of the secret service, who would inform me about certain matters. But communication with Jasarevic was really infrequent, at least as it concerned his activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to clarify from your last answer. I'm not sure whether you're saying that you actually spoke to him about Grabovica or you didn't. You said: "What I did say was only an act of courtesy between our two institutions." Are you saying you spoke to him about Grabovica or you didn't speak to him about Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did tell him that I'd been to see the superior officers about the incident in Grabovica. So the reason I called was to tell him that I'd been to see those people to discuss the problem of Grabovica. When I talked to him, I told him also what had happened in Grabovica. I didn't seek or expect any reaction from him because it would not have been logical to expect that. I understood that General Jasarevic, too, was familiar with the case, but it was just a matter of courtesy. That was why I phoned him, too, although it wasn't strictly necessary, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What powers or authorities did the civilian police or MUP employees have to investigate crimes allegedly committed by members of the military?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police had no powers over any members of the army, and here I mean first and foremost members of the army who were actually members of military units, and you can take it from there on, combat operations, manoeuvres carried out by certain units. They were under their own superiors, their own commanders, and they answered to their own superiors and commanders. Our only powers concerned cases where they were at a given point in time civilians and, as civilians, committed any violations. That's when we would have powers over them. But we had no special powers, and there were documents and orders to this effect. There were also oral instructions that the police should not interfere in areas of combat activity. I think the same applies in all the armies in the world, that the police have no powers in an area where there is combat going on. So the same applied to the BH MUP. This is not only in reference to our present case; I'm talking about a general principle here that applied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the police have power to initiate their own investigation into the murders in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of its function and under the law and based on any documents governing the work of the police, the police would have had power as well as the duty to carry out any investigations on the operative level; collecting intelligence and security-related information. And here first and foremost I have in mind the state security service. As for the public security service, I think they had no power or authority and they couldn't have had any unless the army had asked them to give them a hand in some way. The intelligence service - and this was another part of the ministry - had the authority to collect information. And it was based on that that they collected information on this incident as well as other incidents that occurred during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which body or organ had the authority or power to investigate the murders in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer specifically, but it must have been military bodies and military judicial bodies that were operational in Bosnia at the time. If not military, then probably it was the civilian judicial bodies. So it would have been the military judicial bodies or the civilian judicial bodies that should have reacted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which body or organ would have been responsible for conducting an investigation into the murders of Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, in light of the witness's last answer, I submit that he shouldn't be pressed for another try at that same question. He's indicated that he can't answer specifically but it must have been a military body. Now, this is simply another way of asking the same question, and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that the witness has already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just give me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the civilian police ever participate in investigations into crimes committed by the military?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in some, pursuant to requests by the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Trial Chamber how that worked, what the role of the military was and what the role of the civilian police were in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only talk about the time of my tenure as minister of the interior. All police activity that had activity within the context of military problems, be it incidents or investigations of certain crimes, would be initiated pursuant to a request by the army. In principle, the military intelligence service or the military police would file a written request or make a direct request, and then this would be recorded, for assistance in whichever way they needed. And they would request specific police resources. This would always be specified. For example, there would need to be an investigation or an expert opinion provided. Resources that the Ministry of the Interior had at its disposal at the time to a greater degree than perhaps the army, as the army was still in the process of setting up these departments and lacked the resources, especially in terms of equipment. In the early days of the war, the ministry often helped the army and solved problems together with the army, but it was the military security bodies who were in charge of the implementation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the last part of your answer, do you mean the military security bodies maintained control of the investigation that civilian police were participating in?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the respective roles of the military police or the military security bodies and the civilian police in any investigation that the civilian police participated in? I mean, what did the military do and what did the civilian police do?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This depended on the case in hand. No two cases were the same. If the perpetrators were military men, then they would be dealt with by the military; the military police would arrest them and detain them and everything else.
