They would have been under the jurisdiction of the army. Any other act that was investigated, if the Ministry of the Interior had better resources, then this would be done in the presence of the police. Documents would then be drafted that were later used in prosecuting these cases. Sometimes an investigating magistrate would be part of the investigation. And you would always need to have a proper team - the composition of this team was defined by regulations - and then documents would be drawn up in relation to the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to be a little bit more specific, if you can. What was the division of responsibilities? I mean, what did the military police do and what did the civilian police do in these investigations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to that. Your Honours, my learned friend already elicited from this witness that he wasn't sure which military body it was that had the -- had the competence to deal with the particular investigation we are dealing with. And in my submission, this is just a third way of doing -- of asking the same question. But if my learned friend has a specific case which this witness knows about and can give an illustration of what happened in that case, then that might give a focus to the question. I wouldn't object to that being done; it might help the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that may be a good suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The witness has said that the military would -- military police would arrest them and detain them and everything else. He's already given an answer as to what the military police do. I'm asking him what the civilian police do. I don't understand the objection. I've asked him about the respective roles. He said the military police arrest and detain. Well, I'm asking him what the civilian police do in these investigations which are under the control of the military but in which the civilian police participate. Now, he's the minister of interior, in charge of all the police in Bosnia at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: If my friend will stop there, I'll indicate this: If that's the question, if that's the question, I've got no objection to it at all. What do the civilian police do in such a case? I don't object to that. Of course the witness knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the question.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First there is the assumption that the military seek assistance from the police in one of these tasks. There is the tasks that they are setting out to do, there must be an on-site investigation, and an on-the-spot assessment must be made. So the army makes a request for the police to give assistance. The request would usually specify the kind of assistance being sought from the police; what the police is supposed to do, in other words. Everything else, with the exception of the army, would have been under the jurisdiction of the police. Everything to do with citizens, with the protection of property, would have been within the remit of the police. As far as military persons are concerned, then it would be down to other bodies to carry out investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Securing the crime scene, whose responsibility was that; the military police or the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police. If there is an incident in the area of combat operations, if there is an incident wherever the army is staying, if there is an incident with soldiers as the perpetrators, the crime scene is secured by the army and everything else is done by the army. And the police, I think the best expression would be, assists, perhaps, in as far as any assistance is requested, it offers whatever assistance it can. But it is the army that sees the task through from the very beginning to the very end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the collecting of forensic evidence, such as taking photographs, fingerprints, footprints, blood testing, or any of those sorts of things? Civilian police or military police?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to add the following, in order to explain it in simple terms: If the civilian police would have to apprehend a soldier, civilian police cannot come in and take in a soldier for interrogation. Civilian police cannot apprehend and take into custody a soldier. Under no circumstances can this be done by civilian police, because there is a separate structure in charge of the soldiers. Since the Ministry of the Interior, even before the war, had decent equipment and very good personnel trained to carry out on-site investigations and was competent for all of the technical issues relating to investigation, then in the territory of the BH they would go to the sites jointly in order to carry an examination and possibly identify the perpetrators. It could involve an ordinary robbery, a brawl involving -- or resulting in death. So there are a lot of elements here that need to be taken into account. Various experts need to be consulted. This just shows you how complex this issue is. And the police did a lot and assisted a lot, provided a lot of assistance to the army in order for the army to create its own service. And nowadays the BH army has all of these facilities within its own framework, but at the time they had neither the staff required nor the equipment in order to carry out the job. And in that sense, the Ministry of the Interior assisted them, when it comes to matters that represent the core of its work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about autopsies and exhumations? Was the military equipped to do that in 1993 when you were the minister of the interior, or did they have to rely on Ministry of the Interior support for that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in general terms, in order to conduct autopsies and exhumations, there was a division that was established in the context of investigating war crimes. This division functioned within the BH government and conducted exhumations. As for other medical expertise, they used the services of the experts within the hospital centre of Sarajevo in order to conduct autopsies and so on, because at the time neither the army nor the Ministry of the Interior had appropriate services within their own framework.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the taking of witness statements in a military investigation in which civilian police were participating? Were the civilian police authorised to take witness statements?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian police was authorised only if the army asked it to get involved. It could not get involved on its own. It could not conduct investigation against any members of the army. The police needed a prior consent of the military, or a request in order to get involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what I'm -- what about the taking statements from civilians in such an investigation?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry could take statements from civilians and then forward them to the military organs, if they were related to the investigation conducted by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Telephone tapping, was that something within the province of your ministry?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the legal process by which telephone tapping was undertaken? How was it authorised?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for tapping to be put in place, that fell under the jurisdiction of the SDB, the state security service. The service had to submit a justification, a statement of reasons why this measure had to be applied. So the reasons had to be stated in a document, and the document needed to be signed by three persons: The operative officer, the lowest-ranking one who proposed this measure; then the chief of the security service who approved it; and finally, the minister who also gave his consent. All of these measures of the secret service, including the wire-tapping, had to be verified by political circles, meaning the head of state. Secret wire-tapping at the operative level could be approved by the minister and the chief of the secret service. Those were the regulations in force at the time, the ones that were applied at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the military or military security service have the capacity to undertake telephone surveillance - that's telephone tapping - in 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in 1993 the army did not have such capabilities, and even within the SDB this was quite limited because we had suffered severe physical damage of the PTT system. So our capabilities were limited. This was not always possible for technical reasons. I think that the army, towards the end of the war, or perhaps in 1996 and 1997, procured some of that equipment for themselves as well. And until that time, they used our resources, the resources of the state security service, which is actually a service that we provided to them, the SDB provided that service to the army. Because this was a security problem, and at the time any security problem was treated as a problem of these two services when it comes to the application of this measure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Mr. Halilovic's phone; was it tapped in 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, his telephone was tapped. It was listened-in to during one period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But who requested and who authorised the interception of Mr. Halilovic's telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to that, I would have to give you another explanation, if possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you -- as you asked about this measure, in 1993 -- I was given advice to speak in this manner. To go back to the issue, this was 1993 and it involved sensitive measures of the secret service. I took the office of the minister in June of 1993. Upon acquainting myself with the secret security service where the focus was directed at ensuring that it operated legally, it was established that certain measures of that service were put in place against Sefer Halilovic before my appointment by Munir Alibabic, who at the time was the chief of the secret service sector in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What I want to know is: When you were the minister, was Mr. -- You said Mr. Halilovic's phone was tapped. Who had requested the tapping of his phone and who had authorised it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one more sentence, with your permission, because I believe this to be important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, and then the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. All of the measures of the secret service, all wire-tapping, after this review, were terminated, meaning they were not applied any more. This was one of the first moves of the then-chief of the secret service who had to clean-up, so to speak, the service. The situation was very grave in 1993. So wire-tapping, not only of General Halilovic but of others, was discontinued as well. And this is something that can be verified in the documentation in Sarajevo. The measure was re-applied in relation to General Halilovic at the request of the military intelligence service and upon consent by President Izetbegovic. I think that there must be a document confirming this in the archives of the state security service and the military security service, because the office -- or the post held by General Halilovic, and General Halilovic himself, were so important, it was believed that the measure had to be applied properly. So the chief of the secret service himself was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The request, you said, was from the military intelligence. Was that from Mr. Jasarevic himself?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it did come from Jasarevic, that he was the chief of service at the time, although the people in that post rotated. But I think that this was during the time when the service was led by Jasarevic. 10

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now it's time for us to take a break and we'll resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about the telephone tapping of Mr. Halilovic's phone before the break. What was the reason for the request to tap his telephone?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time when the telephone was wire-tapped -- I think I need to explain this in more detail. The request had arrived from the military security service, and the explanation was that problems had to be resolved, problems relating to the units in town which had already caused a number of problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which unit?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones that I spoke about in the beginning. The brigades under the command of Caco, Celo, and some smaller formations. So it involved them, and then the incident in Grabovica was something that topped it all. The military structures and the Presidency decided that the problem had to be tackled. And I think that it was in the context of that operation, of that campaign that the military service requested that General Halilovic's phone be tapped because, as they said, he had contacts with some officers such as Celo, Delalic, and some others whose names I can't remember now. But all of these names are stated in the documents. These contacts were seen as a potential security problem, something that was important in order to resolve the situation. And the authorities simply wanted to have a clearer picture of the role and position of General Halilovic in relation to these commanders and units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any other senior military officers' telephones tapped at that same time, or was it only Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several phones were tapped. I can't claim with certainty -- I can't give you the specific names of people whose phones were tapped, but these were definitely the members of the army who were of interest to the security service, who caused problems or had contacts with problematic persons. And as a result of that, the security service deemed it appropriate to apply the measure, or rather to request that the SDB apply the measure. At the time, the situation was very difficult. The war was going on and the situation in Sarajevo was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is people of Mr. Halilovic's seniority or below his, like members of the command -- Supreme Command staff or corps commands or people of that level of seniority. Are you able to say now whether the telephones of any of those people were tapped?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, General Halilovic was the most senior military officer whose phone was tapped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there was only one above him in the army, that's Mr. Delic. What about the people on the level below him, like corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the measure is applied on the basis of the post or function, no. I think the measure is applied if there are reasons to believe that the person could be of interest to security services. The position is irrelevant, be it the position of the chief of the General Staff or the corps commander or the brigade commander. I don't think that the measure is applied on that basis, on the basis of the post held by an officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from telephone interception, was there any other surveillance of Mr. Halilovic by your service or, to your knowledge, the military intelligence or the military security service?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware - and I'm certain that the SDB did not apply any other measure against General Halilovic - that's as far as I know. This is what I can tell you from my domain. Now, as to any other measure applied by the military secret service, I couldn't tell you anything about that. The SDB applied only the wire-tapping measure, and that was done at the request of the military security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the -- does that include interception of radio communications or are you confining it to telephone interception?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The measure pertained exclusively to telephone conversations. Interception of radio communications, as far as I know, was a matter that was of general relevance. Everybody could listen to that. The technology was so poor in town that from the transmitter one could pick up various signals, various communications. However, that is not something that was done by the SDB with respect to General Halilovic. The state security service definitely did not apply that measure, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the interception on Mr. Halilovic's telephone and who was responsible for supervising the interceptions?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a purely technical matter. The man who was a professional, who professionally listened to tapped lines, was one of the officers of the SDB. One of the officers was assigned to this task. And pursuant to the SDB regulations, the officer would write up reports detailing how the measure was applied. He was duty-bound to report on that. And the reports were sent only to the chief of the security services, military security services, who would then indicate to whom else the report should be sent, so this is purely a technical matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And very briefly, what was Mr. Enver Mujezinovic's role in the telephone interception?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a purely technical role, and he was not in a position to make any decisions. He could only execute any measures that had been approved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was your role as minister of the interior in Operation Trebevic in late October 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the plan of the Trebevic plan, once it was approved by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I had a position which was a leadership position, and I also had a coordinating role. In accordance with the plan, I was to command the police units which acted together with the military. And as for my coordinating role, I was to coordinate various matters and problems that might arise in the course of the Trebevic operation. The person in charge of the entire operation was General Delic, and in accordance with the document, I was his deputy and I was in charge of the matters that I've just described to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit D261.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wish to raise a matter here. This cross-examination has now expanded way beyond what was in the statement or the proofing notes, and it seems that many matters are now being raised. Frankly, we've all been in the case a long time so I haven't objected to it. In some respects, we can see what's coming. But if the number there was as I heard it, D261 -- I just can't see it on the list. So I'm caught by surprise by this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise, it should be. It's D261, that's the Operation Trebevic document. I'm just asking the witness if that's the correct document, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, just to confirm. Is it -- I don't have a note as to what it is. Is my friend referring to the team -- the document establishing the team?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, the document of the 25th of October, 1993, signed by Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't have an objection to that being shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But actually the direct examination took a longer time than expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, longer than I expected, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But anyway, the witness provided us with very useful information on certain aspects. I believe that it will be also useful in the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It may even cut down cross-examination quite significantly, you never know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed with your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the document in front of you now, Mr. Alispahic, to the left?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to confirm, looking at that document, is that the document by which you were appointed the deputy of the group which was to direct the Trebevic and Trebevic 2?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your role on the day, that is the 26th of October, 1993? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day I was at work. At this time, my task was to see to it that the plan that had been verified by the Presidency was carried out in cooperation with General Delic, as you can see from this order. It was by coincidence that the office of the Ministry of the Interior was chosen for this. I was there with some members of the staff. We were there and we exercised control over the activities that were to happen in the early morning hours. Therefore, what I was doing on that day, I was there to make sure that the Trebevic plan was carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Ministry of the Interior units were involved in Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were a number of different units. It's very difficult for me to remember specifically. The special units, the Bosna Detachment of the Ministry of the Interior, the Laste Special Unit, and a number of police officers who were assigned. On this particular assignment, an assessment had been made indicating that the situation might turn complex. And it was decided to have more police officers committed to this operation. This is a general statement, but we made further additional statements in our stride on that day as the situation required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 of the document, D261, of the 25th of October, 1993, says: "Use all means at your disposal, including weapons, to bring in Musan Topalovic, Ramiz Delalic, and the others if there is any resistance or opposition." That's Caco and Celo. Did you participate in bringing in either Caco or Celo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to clarify the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Paragraph 5 says -- one of the objectives of the operation, according to this document, was, using all means at your disposal, to bring in - I assume that means arrest - Caco and Celo. What was your participation, if any, in arresting or bringing in either Caco or Celo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My participation was defined by this document, the plan that was made. This is just one paragraph that defined the position that should be taken towards these two senior officers. The order stated that -- or rather, authorisation was given if they resisted that any measures could be used. The Trebevic operation, in essence, was a military action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I want to know is --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was so serious that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only want to know about the arrest of Caco and Celo, what your role was. With Celo, did you have anything to do with his arrest?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrest of Celo and Caco was a complex operation, and it was aggravated by the fact that they in fact resisted. The whole operation had been planned and initiated in total secrecy and there were no leaks until the time the commenced. Once the operation was underway, the commanders under consideration realised immediately what was going on. It is possible that they assumed they would be arrested and brought in, that measures would be taken against them. So what they did was to block their own facilities. They got them well fortified and they put up good resistance. There was a fire fight as a result, in the course of which members of both the police and the army were killed. Sarajevo, as you know, was under siege and there was certain combat operations going on that had been imposed by the enemy. And now the situation inside the town was that there was a clash of -- between the regular forces and the renegades. The arrest of Caco was a highly complex operation. What was eventually done was one of the things that were possible. The former minister, Jusuf Pusina, went and convinced Caco to come to the 1st Corps command. Ramiz Delalic, also known as Celo, also put up a great deal of resistance, and it took a lot to place him under control. So this lasted the whole day, and this entailed a certain amount of combat. Delalic asked to speak to someone from the government or from the Presidency. I think the president or the Prime Minister, Silajdzic, decided that I should go to Celo's command as well as Prime Minister Silajdzic. The atmosphere there was awful. There was a lot of panic and fear. There had been a fire fight, after all. Celo requested to have guarantees that he would not be killed, that he would not be persecuted, as well as other guarantees. He even requested to speak to the president, to be received by the president. At this point we wanted to get the hostage situation resolved. There had already been casualties, especially at Caco's command, the command that Caco had held under siege. Six police officers were killed there. Therefore, we agreed. We provided the guarantees that Delalic had requested. We brought two vehicles and drove to the Presidency building, where Prime Minister Silajdzic probably held additional talks, gave Celo further advice and offered further guarantees, while I went back to the Ministry of the Interior. Both Celo and Caco and many other members of those units were brought in on that occasion. The first two were held at the corps command, where they were interviewed. I believe that as many as around 100 soldiers were brought in on that day, which doesn't necessarily mean that they remained in detention. They were simply brought in in order to ascertain their individual responsibility. I believe 10 or 15 of them were eventually detained and the rest were allowed to go home. The members of those units were held back where it was proved that these members or these units were guilty of criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned some police being killed -- six police officers being killed at Caco's command. How did they die?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that. At all events, Mr. Halilovic was in his flat with -- well, I don't think that's in evidence yet. We know that Mr. Halilovic on the 26th, at all events, is not able to play any role that's relevant to this case here. So what happened at the battle of Caco's, in my submission, is meaningless detail and doesn't assist this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, are there any evidence relevant to our case?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll ask another question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, did Mr. Halilovic have any role in the apprehension of Caco or Celo on the 26th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, for one, am not familiar with any role or position that he held or any task that he had as part of this operation, or activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was requested to be involved in it in any way?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think General Jasarevic or some other military commander -- I'm talking about the day when the operation took place and the situation was complex and grave. So I think one of them asked General Halilovic to use his authority with these people. It was believed, because General Halilovic was a commander and now Chief of Staff, that from the beginning of the war he was part of those structures in Sarajevo, and that regardless of how those people acted, they held General Halilovic in high esteem. But I think on that occasion General Halilovic refused. I think Jasarevic said the general had told him that he did not wish to interfere with our job and that we should just press on and keep doing our job. That was what General Jasarevic told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason -- as briefly as you can tell us, the necessity to conduct this military operation between the 9th and the 10th Brigades in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of police classification, this was self-defence. It was highly critical that this problem be solved. It's for truth's sake that I must say this. On that day, even if General Halilovic had interceded with these people, it is highly questionable whether he could have achieved anything because the action was underway by this time and it would have been very difficult to control. They had already opened fire. There was an open clash, a fire fight, and it would have been very difficult to achieve anything at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's been some evidence that -- General Karavelic gave evidence that there were 5.000 military employed against the 9th and the 10th in Operation Trebevic. What was your understanding of the necessity to use so many soldiers against units of the Bosnian army at Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer this question in two ways. I'm not certain, but Karavelic, after all, was the corps commander. I'm not certain -- I was saying that 5.000 men were involved. Maybe there was an estimate that 5.000 should be involved. Maybe this was one of the operations. When I say "one of the options," I mean, for example, if the members of these two brigades leave their combat positions and these positions should immediately be taken by other soldiers. In this eventuality, the estimate was probably justified, but I can't be certain because I'm talking from my own perspective. But I was convinced at the time, and I still am, that there was a real need for this operation to be carried out, implemented, if you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Sefer Halilovic arrested as part of Operation Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the Ministry of the Interior, Sefer Halilovic was never arrested, not according to our norms and criteria, not in terms of what the word "arrested" implies to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's been some evidence that he was interviewed at MUP headquarters from the end of October through mid-November 1993. Why was he interviewed there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general was interviewed following a request of the military service, and this request was approved by the state president. It was done at the state security service centre, and the interview was done by Enver Mujezinovic. The idea was that this service had people who were better qualified to interview a person, a commanding officer, of General Halilovic's rank and standing. Although, as far as I know, the interview lasted many days and members of the military police, or rather members of the army's intelligence service were also involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in custody at the time when he was being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object to that. Your Honours, that cannot be relevant to the charges before the Tribunal now to go into this area. There was a time previously when the Prosecution wanted to lead certain evidence. They led evidence that they wanted to lead then, there was a ruling about it, we've all acted on that ruling since that time. Now, I submit that, at all events, the game was over on the 26th of October, and this is now irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The relevance is this, Your Honours, and that is that we anticipate the Defence case will be, from their pre-trial brief and questions asked of Prosecution witnesses, we anticipate that part of the case is that there was a political campaign or vendetta being conducted against Mr. Halilovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I object to this in the presence of the witness if that's going to be explained like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have no objection to the witness leaving for the purposes of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I would like to say that this Tribunal is to address the personal criminal responsibilities rather than some political issues involved in this matter. It is very important for us to establish that after the 26th of October Mr. Halilovic was arrested and interviewed. And another matter is that: What's the situation after Mr. Halilovic was released, which is not quite clear, or whether Mr. Halilovic resumed his function as the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just checking that it's in evidence yet. My learned friend can stop me if I'm wrong, but I think it is already in evidence - if it's not we'll put it there - that he was removed from his position as Chief of Staff by presidential order, I think on the 1st of November. And -- if you'll just excuse me a moment, Your Honour, we'll tell you the date. It's Exhibit 263, I'm instructed, Your Honour, that by virtue of that order he was removed as Chief of Staff on the 1st of November. Thereafter he's, I think, placed in the position of being at the disposal of the army, and they didn't find -- well, there's no -- I don't think it's going to be suggested they found a job for him. So the 1st of November is the time when he ceases formally to be Chief of Staff. That's one date we can be sure of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It seems to me that it's not necessary for us to go into the very details concerning of the interviews and the conditions in which Mr. Halilovic is interrogated during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I wasn't intending to go anywhere near the interviews. The only thing I wanted to clarify was whether he was in custody at the time of the interviews, and that's up until the time he was dismissed as the chief of the Main Staff, and that's the 1st of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I don't object to him asking that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Halilovic in custody when he was interviewed by your service and the military security service?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Ministry of the Interior was concerned, the general was not in custody. Every day, or whenever agreed, he would arrive in his own vehicle with his driver at the state security premises, where the interview was conducted. This is how the state security treated General Halilovic. As regards the Ministry of the Interior, as far as the Ministry of the Interior was concerned, General Halilovic was never arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about Sefer Halilovic badges? Were there such items?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for a brief while some members sported these badges, some sort of a round badge. I believe that with some of us it caused a certain amount of derision. It was derisory that some people should be wearing the general's badges, which were a sign of revolt by some members around town caused by the removal of General Halilovic and the appointment of General Delic in that post. But I, myself, didn't consider that a real security problem. It was probably just the case that certain members of the army used this as an expression of support for General Halilovic, and I still believe this was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the badges look like? What was on them?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it just had the general's face or effigy, I'm not sure which is the correct expression, the sort you can buy in a shop. You can pin it onto your uniform or onto your lapel. But this wasn't frequent. It wasn't used very much. I remember that Nedzad Ugljen, the former state security chief, once showed me one of these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was making them?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which units were -- you said members of the army were wearing them. Which units were they from?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think most of them were from Delalic's unit. I believe that at the time General Halilovic and the commander of that unit had a good relationship, and I believe that that was where the gesture originated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone yourself wearing these badges in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from once laying eyes on this badge, I didn't really see anyone else. You needed to move about town in order to see it, but I did see this one. I didn't really have too much time to walk around the streets, so I can't say I noticed any badges, but then again you didn't see too many soldiers moving about either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution 65 ter Exhibit 154, which is 0218-3114.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to show you a two-page document dated the 11th of October, 1993. It's a MUP SDB document entitled "Information" and signed by the SDB sector chief, Enver Mujezinovic. What sort of document is that, Mr. Alispahic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an information dealing with a certain security situation or phenomenon, and it is used for further steps by the military leadership or perhaps chief of the security service or the Minister of the Interior. These are the end users of this information that should be a document of high quality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a document -- I'm sorry. It's -- the name on the bottom is Mr. Mujezinovic. What does that indicate to you, the fact that his signature and name is on it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the then-chief of the Sarajevo sector, Enver Mujezinovic, signed the document. This is one of the organisational units which in the course of its work collects certain information of security nature and is further sent to other people. In this specific case, it was sent to the chief of the CSB security services centre, chief of the military -- chief of the secret service, and the minister of the interior. Based on what we can see here, several issues were dealt with in this information. According to the service, all of this information here was relevant from a security point of view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a document that you saw or would have seen as the minister of the interior in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: They should ask the first question first, and that is: Did he see it? And then afterwards we can decide whether he would have seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing this particular document when you were the minister of the interior, in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document definitely reached me. I think that after I saw this document, the chief of the service saw it as well and it could have been also sent to the military security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or rather, the military intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to comment upon the reliability of the information contained there as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just excuse me a minute. Your Honours, once again, that really is your job, to decide on the reliability. What the witness can be asked is: Who provided that information? How far removed from him is the source?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may ask some questions about the source of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the sources used to compile the information in this document?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the document, one can see that Mufid Memija was one of the sources for the document, because the security organ stated here that he was one of the problems, as General Halilovic described him, because he was creating a media ban or a media gag and was not allowing the information to reach the media. And I think that Salko Gusic or somebody else from the military structure explained the contact of General Halilovic in this context. In the subheading you can see what this document is about, namely it is stated here "Indicative attempts by Sefer Halilovic to promote his military successes in the media." So the service believed that this is something that others had to be informed about. The text itself states that the information comes from a reliable source. If one wanted, we could use the number stated in this document in order to identify the source. If one went through the records, we should be able to find that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the denotion of the source as a "reliable source" indicate to you in your experience as the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A reliable source can be a document which leaves no doubt about a fact. It could also be a person who is an associate of the service and is considered to be a reliable associate by the service. It could also be a radio communication, or any other means of communication, or a secret tapping which was not aimed at that person. What I'm trying to say is that through secret wire-tapping of persons who are interesting for the security service, one can obtain information about persons whose communication is not wire-tapped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the source in relation to Zulfikar Alispago, that he had, on Sefer's orders, "bribed certain journalists to report positively on successes of the army under Halilovic's command." Do you know what the source for that was?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I could tell you anything about that. It is very difficult to say what the source was for this segment. It could be Zulfikar Alispago himself; he could be the source. He could have said to some members of the secret service that he had done that. It is stated in the information that this needs to be looked into, but it would be difficult to claim this with any certainty right now. It would be best to check this with Zulfikar Alispago. If it were up to me, I would verify this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on the accuracy or reliability or otherwise of the information in that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, once again the witness should not be put in the position of having to do that; that's really up to you, the Tribunal, to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Based upon what he knows, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have come across this issue already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I move to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, since he's seen the document, there can be no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. This document is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P434.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I only want to show the witness two more documents and ask him to comment on the type of document and I will be finished. The first one is P212 and the second one is P415.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the document's -- is the document there yet? While the document's coming, I just want to ask you something to clarify something from earlier when you said that the military security -- or military police could assist -- request assistance from the civilian police to investigate. Could a military commander do the same; that is, request assistance from the civilian police to investigate crime?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, any senior officer of the BH army could go to the police and get a response to any request, or rather get an assistance. I think that in fact we had quite a good cooperation going on. All of the requests coming from the army were always given a priority, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now please turn to the document which is on the screen, which is P212, a Ministry of the Interior document of the 2nd of November, 1993, headed "Report on negative conduct and activities of Sefer Halilovic, Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the BH armed forces." I just want your brief comment on the type of document this is, that is, its status within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was compiled on the basis of cooperation of the Ministry of the Interior and the Supreme Command staff and the security administration. I think that this information was produced in two copies, or three copies. I don't think that more copies were made. This document was marked as "state secret," and it -- upon being used by whoever it was addressed to, it had to be sent back. The police and the army obtained this information, which they described as negative aspects in the conduct of General Halilovic. I read this on behalf of the Ministry of the Interior; General Delic, Jusuf Jasarevic read this on behalf of the army; and I think that Alija Izetbegovic also was sent this information, and perhaps some other politicians as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Exhibit P415, that is a document dated the 16th of October, 1993. It's a Ministry of the Interior security services centre Sarajevo document, subject: "Overview of security-related information regarding illegal activities and abuse of authority by Ramiz Delalic," with the heading "Official secret, highly classified." Again I want you to tell the Trial Chamber what sort of document this is. What is its status within the security apparatus?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, in a way, provides an overview of security-related information. There were various types of security-related information, and it was based on the work of the state security service, which is duty-bound to collect such information and to inform superiors about it. I think that this document had to reach the chief of the state security service and the chief of the military intelligence service. In my view, this is a document with a high degree of accuracy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the document at the time?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I had this document at the time. I only had collective information and I described to you a little bit ago. However, the contents of this document were sent to me through other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I've just been informed that it is actually still only MFI 415. It wasn't actually admitted into evidence. I would move to tender the document into evidence through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would you just excuse me for one moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I do object to that one. This, I think, is one of the documents outstanding from the previous witness as well, which has to be discussed. And perhaps we can deal with it at that time, Your Honour. But I object to it; the witness didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could delay the debate for the admission of this document into the evidence at a later stage, but of course this document as well as document 150 are pending at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be the evidence in-chief. The only thing I could do is develop further from this witness the contents of the document and so on, but I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think at the end of the testimony of this witness we'll spend some time on those documents. At that time, you may ask some further questions concerning of this document. Well, Witness, I'm afraid that we have to stop here because the time allocated to us for today is over. And we might not sit tomorrow. Madam Usher will show you out of this courtroom, and I hope you still remember what I reminded you of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, is it all right for us not to sit tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are hoping, as I indicated, to get a report from our man in Sarajevo, who can indicate what the position is about those documents. I mean, we reserve our position -- I must say I have an open mind about what the situation is with those, but I don't -- Your Honour, can I just indicate I don't intend to start a fire just to put it out again. So it may be that it's -- one option we're considering is quite a short cross-examination here. So we'll see how it unfolds. But, Your Honours, would it be convenient if we advise the Chamber at around 5.30 today as to what the progress is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And we'll effectively keep the Prosecution advised, of course, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage this Bench has a ruling to make, which is concerning of the decision on the Defence motion concerning use and the tendering of a new military expert report filed on the 23rd May, 2005. On the 31st of March, 2003, the Prosecution filed the expert opinion of Major General Matthew Ridgway. During the Status Conference of the 28th April, 2005, the Prosecution indicated that it would seek to tender Mr. Ridgway's report into evidence and call him to testify before this Trial Chamber. By letter of 12th May, the Prosecution provided the Defence with a version of Mr. Ridgway's report that was revised by the Prosecution. The revised version of the expert report was received by the Trial Chamber on the 13th of May, 2005. On the 13th May, 2005, the Defence filed its motion concerning use and the tendering of the military expert report, in which the Defence objected to the expert report in its original or revised form to be used at trial and to be admitted into evidence; it also objected to the calling of Mr. Ridgway as an expert witness. The matter was also discussed in the Court on the 12th and 13th of May. On the 18th May, 2005, the Prosecution filed its response to the Defence motion concerning use and the tendering of the military expert report, in which the Prosecution, having reviewed the expert report in the light of the Defence objection, informed the Trial Chamber that it no longer intends to rely upon the report in its entirety or in a revised form. The Prosecution stated that it accepts that it now would be impractical at this stage of the trial to expect an expert witness to properly digest summaries of the evidence and many additional documents and to formulate a response which could appropriately assist the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber, therefore, considers the Defence request in a motion of 13th May, 2005, with regard to admission of the expert report as moot. In the response, the Prosecution also outlined the proposed scope of expert testimony and indicated that it would provide Defence with a short opinion of Mr. Ridgway by 20th May, 2005. On the 20th May, 2005, the Prosecution filed a new expert opinion of Lieutenant General Matthew Ridgway. On the 23rd May, 2005, the Defence filed its motion concerning the use and the tendering of a new military expert report, in which it objects both to be used and the admission of the new expert report and to -- and to the calling of Mr. Ridgway as an expert witness. The Prosecution responded to the Defence motion concerning the new expert report during the trial hearing on the 23rd May, 2005. The Trial Chamber has considered the arguments submitted by both parties. The Trial Chamber finds that the disclosure of the new report at this late stage of proceedings does not accord with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Its admission would cause prejudice to the accused and it would be contrary to the fundamental requirement of a fair trial. Moreover, the relevance of the new report to the present case is doubtful, and the Trial Chamber finds that the report and proposed testimony of Mr. Ridgway would not be of assistance to the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber therefore decides pursuant to Article 21(4)(b) and Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence not to admit the expert report and not to hear the testimony of Mr. Ridgway as an expert witness in the present case. It is so decided. The hearing for today is adjourned, and we'll see you the day after tomorrow.
